units.title: Big O Analysis
units.tip: Big O measures how an algorithm's performance scales with input size. O(1) is constant, O(n) grows linearly, O(n^2) quadratically. Lower is faster. Understanding Big O helps you choose efficient algorithms.

exercises.question: What does Big O notation measure?
exercises.answer: How an algorithm's performance scales as input grows
exercises.explain: Big O ignores constants and focuses on the dominant term. It predicts how performance changes with larger inputs.
choices: The number of lines of code
How an algorithm's performance scales as input grows

exercises.question: What does O(1) complexity mean?
exercises.answer: Constant time, independent of input size
exercises.explain: O(1) means the time is the same no matter how large the input is. Array access by index is O(1).
choices: Constant time, independent of input size

exercises.question: What does O(n) complexity mean?
exercises.answer: Time grows proportionally with input size
exercises.explain: O(n) is linear. Doubling the input size doubles the time. Linear search is O(n).
choices: Time grows proportionally with input size

exercises.question: What does O(log n) complexity mean?
exercises.answer: Time grows logarithmically with input size
exercises.explain: O(log n) is very efficient. Doubling input size increases time only slightly. Binary search is O(log n).
choices: Time grows logarithmically with input size

exercises.question: What does O(n^2) complexity mean?
exercises.answer: Time grows quadratically with input size
exercises.explain: O(n^2) means nested loops. Doubling input size multiplies time by 4. Bubble sort is O(n^2) in worst case.
choices: Time grows quadratically with input size

exercises.question: Which complexity is best?
exercises.answer: O(1), then O(log n), then O(n)
exercises.explain: Faster is better. O(1) is constant and fastest. O(log n) is very fast. O(n) is linear. O(n^2) is slow.
choices: O(1), then O(log n), then O(n)

exercises.question: What is O(n log n) complexity?
exercises.answer: Time grows as n times log n, between linear and quadratic
exercises.explain: O(n log n) is efficient and common in sorting. Merge sort and quicksort (average case) are O(n log n).
choices: Time grows as n times log n, between linear and quadratic

exercises.question: For an input of size 1000, which is faster: O(n^2) or O(n log n)?
exercises.answer: O(n log n) is much faster
exercises.explain: O(n^2) = 1,000,000 operations. O(n log n) ≈ 10,000 operations. Logarithmic factors matter hugely.
choices: O(n log n) is much faster

exercises.question: What is the difference between average and worst case?
exercises.answer: Average case is typical performance; worst case is the slowest possible
exercises.explain: Quicksort is O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case. Stating both cases is more accurate than just one.
choices: Average case is typical performance; worst case is the slowest possible

exercises.question: What is space complexity?
exercises.answer: How much extra memory an algorithm uses relative to input size
exercises.explain: Space complexity measures auxiliary memory, not the input itself. Merge sort is O(n) space; bubble sort is O(1).
choices: How much extra memory an algorithm uses relative to input size

units.title: Arrays and Linked Lists
units.tip: Arrays store elements at fixed positions accessed by index in O(1) time. Linked lists chain nodes together, making insertion O(1) but access O(n). Each has trade-offs.

exercises.question: What is array indexing complexity?
exercises.answer: O(1) constant time
exercises.explain: Arrays store elements contiguously. Index 5 is computed directly: base_address + 5 * element_size. Always instant.

exercises.question: What is array insertion at the end complexity?
exercises.answer: O(1) amortized
exercises.explain: Appending to the end of an array is usually O(1). When capacity is full, it reallocates and copies (O(n)), but this happens rarely.

exercises.question: What is array insertion in the middle complexity?
exercises.answer: O(n) because elements shift
exercises.explain: Inserting at position 5 requires shifting all elements after it. In the worst case, you shift every element.

exercises.question: What is array deletion complexity?
exercises.answer: O(n) because remaining elements shift
exercises.explain: Deleting position 5 requires shifting all elements after it leftward. Worst case is O(n).

exercises.question: Why is array search O(n) without sorting?
exercises.answer: You must check each element until you find it
exercises.explain: Linear search has no choice but to look at every element in worst case. Found at the end? O(n).
choices: You must check each element until you find it
Arrays can only search the first element

exercises.question: What is a linked list?
exercises.answer: A chain of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next
exercises.explain: Each node contains a value and a reference to the next node. No contiguous memory required.
choices: A chain of nodes, each holding data and a pointer to the next

exercises.question: What is linked list access complexity?
exercises.answer: O(n) because you traverse from the head
exercises.explain: To access the 5th node, you start at the head and follow pointers 5 times. No direct indexing.
choices: O(n) because you traverse from the head

exercises.question: What is linked list insertion at the head complexity?
exercises.answer: O(1) constant time
exercises.explain: Create a new node, point it to the current head, and update the head. No shifting needed.

exercises.question: What is linked list insertion in the middle complexity?
exercises.answer: O(n) because you must traverse to the position
exercises.explain: Even though insertion itself is O(1), finding the position requires traversing O(n) nodes.
choices: O(n) because you must traverse to the position

exercises.question: What is the main advantage of linked lists over arrays?
exercises.answer: Fast insertion/deletion when you have a pointer to the location
exercises.explain: Once you are at a node, inserting or deleting neighbors is O(1). Arrays require O(n) shifting.
choices: Fast insertion/deletion when you have a pointer to the location

units.title: Stacks, Queues, and Hash Tables
units.tip: Stacks are LIFO (last in, first out). Queues are FIFO (first in, first out). Hash tables map keys to values using a hash function. Hash tables offer O(1) average lookup, collision handling varies.

exercises.question: What is a stack?
exercises.answer: A LIFO collection: last element in is first out
exercises.explain: Think of a stack of plates. You remove from the top, the last one placed. push(x) adds, pop() removes.
choices: A LIFO collection: last element in is first out

exercises.question: What operations does a stack have?
exercises.answer: push (add), pop (remove from top), peek (view top)
exercises.explain: push(5) adds 5 to the top. pop() removes the top element. peek() views the top without removing.
choices: push (add), pop (remove from top), peek (view top)

exercises.question: What is a queue?
exercises.answer: A FIFO collection: first element in is first out
exercises.explain: Think of a line. First person in leaves first. enqueue(x) adds to the back, dequeue() removes from the front.
choices: A FIFO collection: first element in is first out

exercises.question: What are the complexities of stack operations?
exercises.answer: O(1) for push, pop, and peek
exercises.explain: All stack operations are constant time. Add/remove from one end, no traversal needed.
choices: O(1) for push, pop, and peek

exercises.question: What are the complexities of queue operations?
exercises.answer: O(1) for enqueue, dequeue, and peek
exercises.explain: Queues maintain two pointers: front and back. Operations at both ends are constant time.
choices: O(1) for enqueue, dequeue, and peek

exercises.question: What is a hash table?
exercises.answer: A data structure mapping keys to values using a hash function
exercises.explain: A hash function converts a key into an array index. hash('name') might return 7, so dictionary['name'] looks at index 7.
choices: A data structure mapping keys to values using a hash function

exercises.question: What is a hash function?
exercises.answer: A function converting a key into an array index
exercises.explain: hash('Alice') returns a number from 0 to table_size-1. The same key always hashes to the same index.
choices: A function converting a key into an array index

exercises.question: What is a hash collision?
exercises.answer: Two different keys hash to the same index
exercises.explain: hash('Alice') and hash('Bob') might both return 5. Collisions must be handled by chaining or probing.
choices: Two different keys hash to the same index

exercises.question: What is collision chaining?
exercises.answer: Storing colliding keys in a linked list at each index
exercises.explain: If hash('Alice') and hash('Bob') both return 5, store a linked list at index 5 with both entries.
choices: Storing colliding keys in a linked list at each index

exercises.question: What is the average-case lookup complexity in a hash table?
exercises.answer: O(1) constant time
exercises.explain: With a good hash function and reasonable load factor, average lookup is O(1). Worst case is O(n) with many collisions.

units.title: Trees and Graphs
units.tip: Trees are hierarchies: root at top, children below. Binary search trees keep left < parent < right for fast search. Heaps maintain an ordering for priority queues. Graphs are networks: nodes connected by edges. BFS explores breadth-first; DFS goes deep.

exercises.question: What is a tree?
exercises.answer: A hierarchical data structure with a root and child nodes
exercises.explain: Each node has a parent (except the root) and zero or more children. No cycles.
choices: A hierarchical data structure with a root and child nodes

exercises.question: What is a binary tree?
exercises.answer: A tree where each node has at most two children
exercises.explain: Binary trees have left and right children. Each child is itself a binary tree.
choices: A tree with exactly two nodes
A tree where each node has at most two children

exercises.question: What is a binary search tree (BST)?
exercises.answer: A binary tree where left < parent < right
exercises.explain: In a BST, all values in the left subtree are less than the parent, and all in the right subtree are greater. Enables fast search.
choices: A tree that is sorted top to bottom
A binary tree where left < parent < right
A tree with exactly three values

exercises.question: What is the search complexity in a balanced BST?
exercises.answer: O(log n) average case
exercises.explain: A balanced BST is similar to binary search on an array. Each comparison halves the search space.

exercises.question: What is a heap?
exercises.answer: A complete binary tree where parent >= all children (max heap) or parent <= all children (min heap)
exercises.explain: Heaps maintain a partial order. The root is always the max (or min). Enables O(log n) insertion and extraction.
choices: A complete binary tree where parent >= all children (max heap) or parent <= all children (min heap)

exercises.question: What is a graph?
exercises.answer: A set of nodes connected by edges
exercises.explain: Graphs are more general than trees. Nodes are called vertices; connections are edges. Cycles are allowed.
choices: A set of nodes connected by edges

exercises.question: What are directed and undirected graphs?
exercises.answer: Directed edges have direction (A to B); undirected edges go both ways
exercises.explain: In a directed graph, edge A->B does not mean B->A. In undirected, if A-B exists, B-A also exists.
choices: Undirected is a special case of directed
Directed edges have direction (A to B); undirected edges go both ways

exercises.question: What is breadth-first search (BFS)?
exercises.answer: Exploring all neighbors before exploring deeper nodes
exercises.explain: BFS uses a queue. Visit root, then all children, then all grandchildren. Explores level by level.
choices: Exploring all neighbors before exploring deeper nodes

exercises.question: What is depth-first search (DFS)?
exercises.answer: Exploring as far as possible along each branch before backtracking
exercises.explain: DFS uses a stack. Go deep into one path, backtrack when stuck, then explore another path.
choices: Exploring as far as possible along each branch before backtracking

exercises.question: What are the complexities of BFS and DFS?
exercises.answer: Both O(V + E) where V is vertices and E is edges
exercises.explain: Both visit every vertex once and traverse every edge once. Linear in the size of the graph.
choices: Both O(V + E) where V is vertices and E is edges

units.title: Searching and Sorting
units.tip: Linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n) on sorted data. Bubble sort is O(n^2) naive. Merge sort is O(n log n) always. Quicksort is O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst. Choose wisely.

exercises.question: What is linear search?
exercises.answer: Checking each element one by one until found
exercises.explain: Start at the beginning and compare each element. Works on any list, but slow on large unsorted data.
choices: Checking each element one by one until found

exercises.question: What is the complexity of linear search?
exercises.answer: O(n) in the worst case
exercises.explain: You might need to check all n elements. Average case is also O(n).

exercises.question: What is binary search?
exercises.answer: Dividing sorted data in half repeatedly to find a target
exercises.explain: Check the middle. If target is smaller, search left half; if larger, search right half. Requires sorted data.
choices: Dividing sorted data in half repeatedly to find a target

exercises.question: What is the complexity of binary search?
exercises.answer: O(log n)
exercises.explain: Each comparison halves the search space. On 1,000,000 items, you need at most 20 comparisons.

exercises.question: When is binary search faster than linear search?
exercises.answer: Always on sorted data with reasonably large input
exercises.explain: Binary search's O(log n) beats linear's O(n) unless the list is very small. Cost of sorting is worth it.
choices: Always on sorted data with reasonably large input

exercises.question: What is bubble sort?
exercises.answer: Repeatedly swapping adjacent elements if they are in wrong order
exercises.explain: Compare neighbors, swap if needed. Repeat until sorted. Largest elements 'bubble' to the end.
choices: Repeatedly swapping adjacent elements if they are in wrong order

exercises.question: What is the complexity of bubble sort?
exercises.answer: O(n^2) in average and worst case
exercises.explain: Nested loops: for each pass, you compare all neighbors. n passes, each O(n), so O(n^2).
choices: O(n^2) in average and worst case

exercises.question: What is merge sort?
exercises.answer: Dividing the list in half, sorting each half, and merging results
exercises.explain: Divide and conquer. Split until single elements, then merge while maintaining order. Always O(n log n).
choices: Dividing the list in half, sorting each half, and merging results

exercises.question: What is the complexity of merge sort?
exercises.answer: O(n log n) in all cases, O(n) space
exercises.explain: Guaranteed O(n log n) time. Divides into log n levels, each level is O(n). Space is O(n) for merging.
choices: O(n log n) in all cases, O(n) space

exercises.question: What is quicksort's complexity?
exercises.answer: O(n log n) average case, O(n^2) worst case
exercises.explain: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions around it, and recursively sorts. Good average, bad if pivot is always extreme.
choices: O(n log n) average case, O(n^2) worst case

units.title: Problem Solving Patterns
units.tip: Recursion breaks problems into smaller versions of itself with a base case. Divide and conquer solves subproblems independently. Dynamic programming reuses solutions to avoid recomputation. Greedy picks locally optimal choices.

exercises.question: What is recursion?
exercises.answer: A function calling itself with a simpler version of the problem
exercises.explain: Recursion breaks problems down. Base case stops it. Example: factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1).
choices: A function calling itself with a simpler version of the problem

exercises.question: What is a base case?
exercises.answer: The condition that stops recursion from continuing
exercises.explain: Without a base case, recursion is infinite. factorial(0) = 1 is the base case for factorial.
choices: The condition that stops recursion from continuing

exercises.question: What is divide and conquer?
exercises.answer: Breaking a problem into independent subproblems, solving each, and combining results
exercises.explain: Merge sort divides the array, sorts halves independently, and merges. Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts.
choices: Breaking a problem into independent subproblems, solving each, and combining results

exercises.question: What is the recurrence relation for binary search?
exercises.answer: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), solving to O(log n)
exercises.explain: Each call halves the problem size and does constant work. This solves to logarithmic time.
choices: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1), solving to O(log n)

exercises.question: What is the recurrence for merge sort?
exercises.answer: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n), solving to O(n log n)
exercises.explain: Merge sort divides into two halves (2*T(n/2)) and merges them (O(n)). This solves to O(n log n).
choices: T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + O(n), solving to O(n log n)

exercises.question: What is dynamic programming?
exercises.answer: Solving a problem by storing solutions to subproblems and reusing them
exercises.explain: Avoid recomputing the same subproblem. Fibonacci: instead of recalculating fib(5) every time, store it.
choices: Solving a problem by storing solutions to subproblems and reusing them

exercises.question: What is memoization?
exercises.answer: Storing computed results to avoid recomputation
exercises.explain: Cache results. If fib(5) was computed, reuse it instead of recalculating. Transforms exponential to polynomial.
choices: Storing computed results to avoid recomputation

exercises.question: What is a greedy algorithm?
exercises.answer: Making the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping for a global optimum
exercises.explain: Greedy picks the best option now without planning ahead. Works for some problems (coin change), fails for others.
choices: Making the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping for a global optimum

exercises.question: When does a greedy approach work?
exercises.answer: When the problem has optimal substructure and the greedy choice leads to the global optimum
exercises.explain: Greedy works for some problems (activity selection, coin change with certain denominations) but not all (0-1 knapsack).
choices: When the problem has optimal substructure and the greedy choice leads to the global optimum

exercises.question: What is the difference between DP and greedy?
exercises.answer: DP reuses subproblem solutions; greedy makes one-shot local choices
exercises.explain: DP is exhaustive and guaranteed optimal. Greedy is fast but not always optimal.
choices: DP reuses subproblem solutions; greedy makes one-shot local choices
